title: Gold Spot Explorer: ranking historical gold ground against bare-earth LiDAR
metaDescription: USGS bare-earth LiDAR picks out creek beds and ravines and scores which one is the source, overlaid with active claims and land status, exported as GPX — all free public data.
dek: Ranks historical gold ground against where the gold actually is, then reads the terrain itself to score which creek bed or ravine is the source.
intro: Gold Spot Explorer ranks historical gold ground against where you actually find it, then reads USGS bare-earth LiDAR to pick out the creek beds and ravines themselves and score which one is the source. It overlays active claims and land status so you know whether you may mine, lifts the terrain into a real 3D mesh, and exports targets as GPX for the field. Every data source is free and keyless, and an in-page AI guide points the map at its own answer, running on local weights so no location data leaves the machine.
why: Deliberately a $0-data project: historical, claim, land-status and LiDAR sources are free and keyless, and the guide runs on local weights, so the only cost is compute I already own — which is exactly what makes an offline field kit on a Raspberry Pi possible later. Public data hosts flake, though, and that shaped the design: one host returned a 502 inside a 200 response, so every remote call is bounded by a short timeout, mirrored against a second host for the same dataset, and parsed rather than trusted. Never treat a 200 as data. Bare-earth LiDAR is also simply the best free prospecting signal available, which is why the terrain read is the core of the tool and not a garnish.

faq.q: Where does the data come from?
faq.a: Free keyless public sources: historical gold ground, active mining claims, land status and USGS bare-earth LiDAR. No API key means no quota, no billing and no expiry surprise in a canyon.

faq.q: What does the in-page AI guide cost?
faq.a: $0 per question. It runs on local weights via ollama (ornith-1.5:9b), so there is no per-token bill and no location data leaves the machine.

faq.q: How do you handle unreliable public APIs?
faq.a: Bound every remote call with a short timeout, keep a mirror host for the same dataset, and parse the response instead of trusting the status code — one host returned a 502 inside a 200, so a 200 is never treated as data.

faq.q: Can you take it into the field?
faq.a: That is the direction: because the data layer is keyless and the guide is local, the same tool can run offline on a small edge machine. Terrain and land lookups have no model in the data path at all.

cta: It runs locally and is free for early users — ask me for access.
